PX457 Assignment 7: Graph Neural Networks and Machine Learned Interatomic Potentials¶

Prof Nicholas Hine and Dr Albert Bartók-Pártay, University of Warwick (2025-2026)¶

Context¶

This assignment focusses on using Graph Neural Networks to represent data in 3D space, specifically for crystalline materials. We will develop our own super-simple Machine Learned Interatomic Potential with some hand-picked data from the Materials Project. Then, we will do some calculations using a pre-trained "foundation" model trained on the entire database of the Materials Project.

This tutorial is adapted from a tutorial on the e3nn website originally written by Mario Geiger. Later sections make use of the Atomic Simulation Environment for performing common tasks with systems of atoms.

1) Environment Setup¶

The model we will write ourselves is based on JAX, e3nn and Nequip, so let us first set up our Python environment includes those.

We also install MACE, a powerful MLIP with a "foundation model" capable of describing many types of system.

We will also need nglview and the underlying ngl package, to visualize structures.

The setup here will take a few minutes the first time you load a new Noteable instance.

2) Setting up the model and dataset¶

Our first Euclidean Neural Network will be based on a very simple dataset of different allotropes of carbon. We will refer to them by their numbering in the Materials Project. The Materials Project is a multi-national effort that has computed the properties of all known inorganic materials and made the data and associated analysis available online.

Every known structure has an index in this project, and we will use four of them as our training set: mp-48, mp-66, mp-169 and mp-47 (links go to Materials Project pages for each material).

Two of them should be familiar: one is graphite, while another is diamond. Another less famous structure is lonsdaleite, while a final one is "rhombohedral graphite", a slightly different symmetry from graphite.

To avoid faffing around with retrieving data via the Materials Project API interface (which requires you to register an account), I have saved you some time by saving the CIF files to be downloaded with the assignment.

Computing Edges¶

The first component needs to be a routine to compute the edges of a graph. The routine takes the positions, cell, and a distance-based cutoff as arguments.

For this we will use the routine neighbour_list from the matscipy package. The positions, cell, cutoff arguments need to be passed in as keyword arguments.

We will request the indices i and j and the shift vector S, by passing quantities="ijS" We will also apply periodic boundary conditions by passing in pbc=np.array([True,True,True])

The code returns three arrays, receivers, senders, senders_unit_shifts.

This should return three arrays: receivers is the i index of each edge, senders is the j index, and senders_unit_shifts is the integer vector S representing the home cell of the sender. Currently these are set to None, you will need to write the call to neighbour_list() that sets them.

In [28]:
from matscipy.neighbours import neighbour_list  # fast neighbour list implementation

def compute_edges(positions, cell, cutoff):
    """Compute edges of the graph from positions and cell."""
    receivers, senders, senders_unit_shifts = (None,None,None)
    # YOUR CODE HERE
    receivers, senders, senders_unit_shifts = neighbour_list(
        quantities="ijS",
        positions=positions,
        cell=cell,
        cutoff=cutoff,
        pbc=np.array([True, True, True])
    )
    receivers = np.array(receivers, dtype=int)
    senders = np.array(senders, dtype=int)
    senders_unit_shifts = np.array(senders_unit_shifts, dtype=int)


    # validation tests
    num_edges = senders.shape[0]
    assert senders.shape == (num_edges,)
    assert receivers.shape == (num_edges,)
    assert senders_unit_shifts.shape == (num_edges, 3)
    return senders, receivers, senders_unit_shifts

Create Graphs¶

We need a routine that can create a graph from provided neighbour list information.

We will create an object of type GraphTuple, from the jraph package. jraph is a library for graph neural networks in jax developed by DeepMind.

The function create_graph should create a graph object from the given positions, cell and energy of the crystal.

The documentation of jraph.GraphsTuple can be found here.

We need to pass in a list of nodes, edges, globals, senders, receivers and the number of nodes and edges.

In [30]:
def create_graph(positions, cell, energy, cutoff):
    """Create a graph from positions, cell, and energy."""
    
    # TODO: call the compute_edges routine you completed above,
    #       to set senders, receivers, senders_unit_shifts:
    # YOUR CODE HERE
    senders, receivers, senders_unit_shifts = compute_edges(
        positions, cell, cutoff
    )

    # In a jraph.GraphsTuple object, nodes, edges, and globals can be any
    # pytree. We will convert the arrays to dicts, to ensure the keys are unique.
    # What matters is that the first axis of each array has length equal to
    # the number of nodes, edges, or graphs.
    
    # positions are per-node features:
    nodes = dict(positions=positions)
    # Unit shifts are per-edge features:
    edges = dict(shifts=senders_unit_shifts)
    # energy and cell are per-graph features.
    globals = dict(energies=np.array([energy]), cells=cell[None, :, :])
    n_node=np.array([positions.shape[0]])
    n_edge=np.array([senders.shape[0]])

    # TODO: call jraph.GraphsTuple to create the graph - see documentation link above
    # YOUR CODE HERE
    graph = jraph.GraphsTuple(
        nodes=nodes,
        edges=edges,
        globals=globals,
        senders=senders,
        receivers=receivers,
        n_node=n_node,
        n_edge=n_edge
    )
    return graph

Create relative vectors¶

The model will need to know the relative vectors between the atoms in the crystal. We already know the positions of the atoms inside the unit cell, but we need to know the relative vectors between the atoms even if they don’t belong to the same cell.

We do this by combining the shift vectors we calculated earlier, with copies of the unit cell for each structure, to generate the total position of each "sender" relative to the origin of the home unit cell. We evaluate these vectors using Einstein summation convention on the operands, with jax's implementation of the numpy einsum routine

Using the Einstein summation convention, many common multi-dimensional, linear algebraic array operations can be represented in a simple fashion.

Finally, we need to convert the result into an IrrepsArray from the e3nn package that transforms like a vector.

In [39]:
def get_relative_vectors(senders, receivers, n_edge, positions, cells, shifts):
    """Compute the relative vectors between the senders and receivers."""
    num_nodes = positions.shape[0]
    num_edges = senders.shape[0]
    num_graphs = n_edge.shape[0]

    # check everything has the right shapes
    assert positions.shape == (num_nodes, 3)
    assert cells.shape == (num_graphs, 3, 3)
    assert senders.shape == (num_edges,)
    assert receivers.shape == (num_edges,)
    assert shifts.shape == (num_edges, 3)

    # We need to repeat the cells for each edge.
    cells = jnp.repeat(cells, n_edge, axis=0, total_repeat_length=num_edges)

    # Compute the two ends of each edge.
    positions_receivers = positions[receivers]
    positions_senders = positions[senders] + jnp.einsum("ei,eij->ej", shifts, cells)
    
    # TODO: form final vectors as difference of these two lists of vectors
    # YOUR CODE HERE
    vectors = positions_receivers - positions_senders

    # Convert these to be e3nn datatypes that transform as vectors
    vectors = e3nn.IrrepsArray("1o", vectors)
    return vectors

3) Using the model¶

Create the Model¶

We are now ready to define the model layer itself. We are basing this on the published "Nequip" architecture.

For that we will use the implementation available at github.com/mariogeiger/nequip-jax. This implementation provides a NEQUIPLayerFlax class that implements the Interaction Block part of the Nequip architecture (the blue box in the figure above). The Embedding, Self-Interaction and Global Pooling parts of the Nequip architecture are not implemented in nequip-jax and we will need to implement them ourselves below.

The class below defines a flax-Module. flax is a neural network library that is built on top of jax. flax provides a Module class that is similar to nn.Module in PyTorch. flax also provides a compact decorator that allows us to define the call method of the Module in a more concise way. See the flax documentation for more details.

You do not need to understand the mathematical background of the model, though the original paper on the Nequip architecture will help if you would like to do so. Have a look through the definition of the Model class, and answer the questions below.

In [41]:
class Model(flax.linen.Module):
    @flax.linen.compact
    def __call__(self, graphs):
        num_nodes = graphs.nodes["positions"].shape[0]
        senders = graphs.senders
        receivers = graphs.receivers

        vectors = get_relative_vectors(
            senders,
            receivers,
            graphs.n_edge,
            positions=graphs.nodes["positions"],
            cells=graphs.globals["cells"],
            shifts=graphs.edges["shifts"],
        )

        # We divide the relative vectors by the cutoff
        # because NEQUIPLayerFlax assumes a cutoff of 1.0
        vectors = vectors / cutoff

        # Embedding: since we have a single atom type, we don't need embedding
        # The node features are just ones and the species indices are all zeros
        features = e3nn.IrrepsArray("0e", jnp.ones((num_nodes, 1)))
        species = jnp.zeros((num_nodes,), dtype=jnp.int32)

        # Apply 3 Nequip layers with different internal representations
        for irreps in [
            "32x0e + 8x1o + 8x2e",
            "32x0e + 8x1o + 8x2e",
            "32x0e",
        ]:
            layer = NEQUIPLayerFlax(
                avg_num_neighbors=20.0,  # average number of neighbors to normalize by
                output_irreps=irreps,
            )
            features = layer(vectors, features, species, senders, receivers)

        # Self-Interaction layers
        features = e3nn.flax.Linear("16x0e")(features)
        features = e3nn.flax.Linear("0e")(features)

        # Global Pooling
        # Average the features over the nodes of each graph
        return e3nn.scatter_sum(features, nel=graphs.n_node) / graphs.n_node[:, None]
In [42]:
def get_initial_params(key):
    init_shape = jnp.ones((1, 28, 28, 1), jnp.float32)
    initial_params = CNN().init(key, init_shape)['params']
    return initial_params

Answer questions about the model.

  1. What are the dimensions of each of the 3 internal layers, and how does each part transform?

  2. What is the purpose of the final global pooling step? (what physical quantity does it evaluate?)

  1. What are the dimensions of each of the 3 internal layers, and how does each part transform?

For the first layer, output_irreps, per node we have 32 scalar channels, 8 vector channels and 8 rank-2 tensor channels. The total numeric feature dimension is in the form of 32 scalars, 24 vectors and 40 tensors. These sum to 96, so the features dimensions is (N, 96). The scalar features are invariant under rotation. The vector features transform as 3D vectors, and the rank-2 features transforms by the $l=2$ representation of SO(3), maintaining E(3) equivariance.

For the second layer, output_irreps = "32x0e + 8x1o + 8x2e", so per node we again have 32 scalar channels, 8 vector channels and 8 rank-2 tensor channels. The total numeric feature dimension is 32 scalars, 24 vector components and 40 tensor components, summing to 96, so the features dimension remains (N, 96). The scalar features are invariant under rotation, the vector features transform as 3D vectors, and the rank-2 features transform according to the $l=2$ representation of SO(3), preserving full E(3) equivariance.

For the third layer, output_irreps = "32x0e", so per node we have 32 scalar channels only. The total numeric feature dimension is therefore 32 scalars, giving features dimension ((N, 32)). All features are rotationally invariant (0e), so the representation is now fully invariant under E(3), suitable for scalar energy prediction.

  1. What is the purpose of the final global pooling step? What physical quantity does it evaluate?

The final global pooling step gathers the scalar predictions into a single graph-level output. By the end, each node has an invariant scalar feature of size (N, 1). The use of scatter_sum sums each node value across each graph, where the mean per node is computing with an output (G, 1) where G is the number of graphs in a batch. The pooling step evaluates the predicted formation energy per atom for each crystal structure, giving an translation, rotation and permutation invariant output.

Define loss function¶

Now that we have defined our model, we need a loss function, in order to train it.

We will use the mean squared error (i.e. square of difference between predictions and targets).

You should ensure you use operations for this from the jax implementation of numpy (jnp).

In [43]:
def loss_fn(preds, targets):
    assert preds.shape == targets.shape
    # TODO: Set the value of "loss", to be the mean squared error
    # YOUR CODE HERE
    loss = jnp.mean((preds - targets) ** 2)
    return loss

Define an optimiser¶

To optimise our model's parameters we will use Adam.

We need to create an instance of optax.adam, passing in learning rate 1e-3, and store the result as opt.

This optimizer needs to keep track of the average of the gradients and the average of the squared gradients, for which it uses a stored state. The state is initialized with opt.init.

In [47]:
# TODO: Initialize the ADAM optimizer with a learning rate of 1e-3
# YOUR CODE HERE

opt_state = opt.init(params)
In [48]:
# Check that you have created the right thing
assert(type(opt)==optax._src.base.GradientTransformationExtraArgs)

Define the training step¶

Let's define a function that is taken each training step, passing in the opt_state, params, and dataset.

First, we compute the loss as a function of the parameters. model.apply() returns the predictions as preds, which are passed to the loss function alongside the known targets

We use jax autograd (via value_and_grad(fun)) to take the gradient of the function with respect to its parameters.

The optimiser opt then handles updating the parameters of the model. The current opt_state, params and loss are then returned.

In [49]:
# TODO: use @jax.jit to compile this function, to make it run faster
# YOUR CODE HERE
@jax.jit
def train_step(opt_state, params, dataset):
    """Perform a single training step."""
    num_graphs = dataset.n_node.shape[0]

    # Compute the loss as a function of the parameters
    def fun(w):
        preds = model.apply(w, dataset).array.squeeze(1)
        targets = dataset.globals["energies"]

        assert preds.shape == (num_graphs,)
        assert targets.shape == (num_graphs,)
        return loss_fn(preds, targets)

    # And take its gradient
    loss, grad = jax.value_and_grad(fun)(params)

    # Update the parameters and the optimizer state
    updates, opt_state = opt.update(grad, opt_state)
    params = optax.apply_updates(params, updates)

    return opt_state, params, loss

Testing the Model¶

There are 64 structures on the MP website containing only carbon - we only defined four of them. Many of them are very similar to each other, but some are completely different. Here is a search for them:

https://next-gen.materialsproject.org/materials?_limit=75&formula=C

I have saved the CIF files for 10 of these in the folder MP_Carbon_CIFs which should get downloaded with the assignment. They have a variety of different bonding: some all-covalent, some with covalent units and van der Waals interactions between layers or molecules.

The names of the structures, and their formation energy above the convex hull, are stored in the dictionary below.

One of them, C_2516584, is what has defined the "Convex Hull" for this stoichiometry: its formation energy is defined as zero, as it is the lowest observed value per atom of all the structures of this same composition.

Discuss the performance of the model¶

Under what conditions does it seem to be reliable as a predictor of the total energy?

For what kind of structures is it unreliable - do they have any common features?

The model is a reliable predictor of total energy when the true formation energy is low and the structures are similar to the training set. This is shown in the plot where the low formation energy test structures have strong predictive performance, so we can deduce that for (near) stable carbon allotropes, this model is suitable. For higher formation energy structures and more complex carbon allotropes, model performance degrades. For example, C_2646980 is significantly underpredicted.

How could we improve the performance of the model?¶

Consider possible changes to model structure, training procedure and the composition of the training set.

Feel free to perform and report and computational experiments you perform by changing the code above, but please reset it before submission to the suggested parameters.

  • Increase the size of the training set and including more carbon structures with the full range of bonds (i.e. van der Waal-bound structures, chain motifs, $sp^2$ sheets, $sp^3$ networks, etc.). Variation should be prevalent throughout the dataset to help with robustness, mainly through reasonable pertubations in structure.
  • The use of holdout layers to help generalisation.
  • Regularisation to mitigate overfitting to the training data, through the use of weights, early stopping during validation, dropout layers.
  • Varying learning rate (i.e. exponential decay).

4) Using the MACE_MP foundation model¶

NB: This section is an optional extra with a low weight in mark scheme (15% of the assignment, which is 15% of the module)¶

Like Nequip, MACE is a state-of-the-art Machine Learned Interatomic Potential, making use of e3nn to achieve data-efficientcy and high-accuracy. There are PyTorch and JAX versions available - the PyTorch version is under more active development at the present time so we will try that here.

https://github.com/ACEsuit/mace

The MACE architecture was first described in 2022, and its innovation was to combine successfully using Atomic Cluster Expansion techniques with Message Passing methods as in Graph Neural Networks.

In late 2023, the MACE team released two papers describing "Foundation Models": one general-purpose organic force field, and one model trained on the entire Materials Project database, for general purpose use on inorganic crystals.

We will try the latter, mace_mp. We will use ASE calculators here. These are quite slow to use in CPU mode, but we will not try them on anything very large here.

These sections are relatively "unstructured". You may have to look up ASE syntax to complete them. They will require self-directed reading from the examples on the ASE website. I would prefer not to be dealing with questions about this section, as it is meant to be an opportunity to discover functionality of a package - not a hand-holding exercise! These sections are not heavily-weighted in the mark scheme (15% of the assignment), so if you do not have time to give them a try, you will not lose much.

Starting from the geometry you optimised, plot the phonon band structure for 100 points along the path $\Gamma-K-M-\Gamma$ for C_2516584, on a 2x2x1 supercell.

You will need atoms.cell.bandpath and get_band_structure from Phonons(). The resulting bs object has its own bs.plot routine which can handle the plotting (you need to set emin and emax to get it to plot a sensible range).

The run will take a while - if you interrupt it you may find a phonon directory that you will need to delete (rm -rf phonon)

If your phonon calculation works out correctly, you should find phonon frequencies in the range 0 to about 0.16 eV - with some negative frequencies actually corresponding to imaginary modes, which represent instabilities.

In [73]:
from ase.phonons import Phonons

atoms = read("MP_Carbon_CIFs/C_2516584.cif")
atoms.calc = calc

phonons = Phonons(atoms, atoms.calc, supercell=(2, 2, 1), name="phonon")
phonons.run()
phonons.read(acoustic=True)

band_path = atoms.cell.bandpath("GKMG", npoints=100)
band_structure = phonons.get_band_structure(band_path)

fig = band_structure.plot(emin=-0.02, emax=0.16)

Initialise the velocities of the C_1008395 model to a Maxwell Boltzmann distribution at 300K, then run Molecular Dynamics for 100 timesteps with the Langevin Thermostat using T=300K, friction=0.01/fs, timestep 2 fs.

Print the initial and final coordinates.

In [77]:
from ase.md.langevin import Langevin
from ase.md.velocitydistribution import MaxwellBoltzmannDistribution
from ase import units

f = "C_1008395"
atoms_ref = read(f"MP_Carbon_CIFs/{f}.cif")
atoms_md = atoms_ref.copy()
MaxwellBoltzmannDistribution(atoms_md, temperature_K=300)

atoms_md.calc = calc
init = atoms_md.get_positions().copy()
print(f"First 5 atoms coordinates: {init[:5]}")

lang_dynamics = Langevin(
    atoms_md, timestep=2.0 * units.fs, temperature_K=300, friction=0.01/units.fs
)

lang_dynamics.run(100)
final_coords = atoms_md.get_positions().copy()
print(f"Final coordinates for the first 5 atoms: {final_coords[:5]}")
# we can quantify drift by taking the norm
displacement = np.linalg.norm(final_coords - init, axis=1)
print(f"Mean displacement: {displacement.mean()}")

5) Summary¶

You have had an opportunity to set up the internal components of a Graph Neural Network making use of Euclidean symmetry. We trained the model on a very small dataset of Carbon Allotropes and showed it could be reasonably predictive of the energy of other Carbon Allotropes.

We also tried the MACE MP foundation model, and showed that it could handle simulation tasks similar to the models you tried. We showed how the Atomic Simulation Environment could be used to handle a variety of simple simulation workflows with a Machine Learned Interatomic Potential.
